name: Viking 2
summary: The twin of Viking 1, a lander that scooped Martian soil to test for signs of life on the flat plains of Utopia Planitia until its last data reached Earth in 1980.
discoveries: Sent back pictures of a remarkably flat Martian plain for more than three years.
Used a robot arm to scoop up soil and test it for signs of life.

stories.kids: I’m Viking 2, twin of Viking 1. We landed on nearly opposite sides of Mars. I used my robot arm to scoop up soil and test it for signs of life, and I sent back pictures. My last data reached Earth in 1980, and I’m still where I landed.
stories.explorer: Viking 2 touched down on Utopia Planitia on September 3, 1976, just after Viking 1 landed on the other side of Mars. The last data from the lander arrived at Earth on April 11, 1980. Viking 1 worked the longest, until 1982.
stories.scientist: Viking Lander 2 touched down at Utopia Planitia (47.64° N, 134.29° E, planetocentric) on September 3, 1976, after the orbiter entered Mars orbit on August 7. The landing area is remarkably flat, with near-field slopes under 1 degree, and lies somewhat near the large crater Mie. The last data from the lander arrived at Earth on April 11, 1980.

image.alt: View from the Viking 2 lander on Utopia Planitia: parts of the lander, a U.S. flag and a flat, rock-strewn Martian plain.

timeline.title: Into orbit
timeline.text: The Viking 2 spacecraft enters orbit around Mars, with its lander still attached.

timeline.title: Touchdown on Utopia Planitia
timeline.text: The lander separates and touches down on a flat plain, then begins sending back pictures and testing soil for signs of life.

timeline.title: The last data
timeline.text: The last data from Viking Lander 2 arrives at Earth. The lander stays where it landed.

learn.title: Who I am
learn.text: I’m Viking 2, the twin of Viking 1. I landed on Utopia Planitia, a vast flat plain on Mars, on September 3, 1976, on nearly the opposite side of the planet from my twin.

learn.title: What I did
learn.text: I sent back pictures of my surroundings, and I used my robot arm to scoop up soil and test it for signs of life.

learn.title: How it ended
learn.text: The last data from me reached Earth on April 11, 1980, after more than three years on Mars. I’m still sitting where I landed.
